UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                          )
    American Transmission Company, LLC                    )             Docket No. ER26-3531
                                                          )

                 MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF THE
                 MIDCONTINENT INDEPENDENT SYSTEM OPERATOR, INC.

          The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) submits1 this Motion for

Leave to Answer and Answer (“Answer”) to the Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer filed by

American Transmission Company LLC by its corporate manager, ATC Management Inc.

(collectively, “ATC”). MISO appreciates ATC’s efforts to reconcile the differing standards

applicable under the MISO Open Access Transmission, Energy, and Operating Reserve Markets

Tariff (“Tariff”) and associated revisions, and ATC’s proposed requirements. Yet, the core issues

identified in MISO’s limited protest and the identified directives are not resolved. Accordingly,

MISO reiterates the concerns noted in its limited protest and its requests that the Commission

direct ATC to revise Attachment FF-ATCLLC either to: (1) align with MISO’s pending

Interconnection Reliability Requirements Proposal (“IRR”) and other large load filings related to

FERC’s Large Load Show Cause Order2 once they are completed; or (2) explicitly provide that

any requirements imposed by Attachment FF-ATCLLC on ATC Large Load are additional to those

applicable to Large Load under the MISO Tariff. As discussed below, MISO also would support


1
      See Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
      (“FERC” or “Commission”) (herein referred to the “Rules of Practice and Procedure”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and
      213 (2026).
2
      Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”). These filings ore
      more specifically identified in MISO’s abeyance motion filed in response to the Show Cause Order and generally
      include the large load related filings that MISO has made or intends to make prior to mid-November of this year.
      See, Motion of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator and the MISO Transmission Owners to Hold
      Proceedings in Abeyance and Request for Shortened Comment Period and Expedited Treatment, Docket No.
      EL26-70-000 (filed Aug. 3, 20226) at 9-13.
 a transitional framework that enables ATC’s revised Attachment FF-ATCLLC to be implemented

until MISO’s implementation of large load requirements and processes are enacted, to allay ATC’s

concerns regarding potential delays.

I.     INTRODUCTION

       MISO acknowledges both the challenges and opportunities presented by the growth of

Large Loads in the MISO region and within ATC’s footprint. All parties should have clear and

uniform base-level rules and frameworks in place to address large load growth in a reliable manner

and without undue cost-shifting. Any mismatch in expectations or requirements within the MISO

region would result in confusion and potential cost-shifts that could—and should—be avoided

through a uniform regulatory standard that establishes minimum requirements. Correspondingly,

MISO requests that the Commission should (1) allow ATC’s requirements only where MISO has

no corresponding requirement, as proposed in the transitional framework discussed below; or (2)

in cases where MISO has an established framework, allow ATC to impose stricter requirements

while maintaining compliance with MISO’s requirements (e.g. establish MISO’s requirements as

a minimum threshold that must be met).           Specifically, MISO’s process and operational

requirements as detailed in the IRR Proposal and other filings in response to the Show Cause Order

should apply to ensure a regional set of standards that, once accepted by the Commission, create

these minimums. An appropriate transition period from ATC’s Attachment FF-ATC framework

to any minimum requirements which vary in MISO’s filings would be acceptable to ensure that no

delays occur due to differences in timing of such filings.

II.    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE ANSWER

       MISO requests permission to submit this Answer to provide additional information related

to the issues raised in ATC’s answer and assist the Commission in its decision-making. Under the




                                                 2
 Commission’s rules, answers to answers generally are not permitted.3                            Nonetheless, the

Commission waives this requirement where an otherwise prohibited answer would clarify the

issues under consideration, ensure completeness of the record or assist the Commission in its

decision-making.4 MISO’s Answer will clarify the issues under consideration, ensure a complete

record, and assist the Commission in its decision-making by detailing the importance of having

uniform base-level rules and avoiding cost-shifts in the MISO region, and by addressing

operational and other issues that will arise if ATC’s proposal is accepted as proposed.

Accordingly, MISO respectfully requests that Rule 213(a)(2) be waived and that the Commission

accept this Answer for good cause shown.

III.       ANSWER

           A.       ATC’s Proposed Tariff Changes Do Not Address the Concerns Raised in
                    MISO’s Answer and Will Create Further Misalignments

           In its Answer, ATC proposes to modify its Large Load definition as follows;

           •    ATC’s large load criteria will apply within the ATC footprint. Large loads over 50MW
                connecting to ATC’s system will be required to comply with MISO’s IRR requirements
                when they become effective if ATC does not have applicable criteria on a given topic.
           •    ATC will modify Attachment FF-ATCLLC and any related business practices to ensure
                that ATC’s large load planning and interconnection criteria will apply to all Large
                Loads over 50 MW.
           •    For Large Loads over 50 MW, ATC will distinguish between computational loads and
                other large loads for power factor and other requirements as deemed necessary by ATC.5




3
       See Rule 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2026).
4
       See, e.g., Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 169 FERC ¶ 61,173, at P 24 (2019) (accepting MISO’s answer
       to protests because it assisted FERC in the decision-making process); Texas Eastern Transmission, LP, 122 FERC
       ¶ 61,205, at P 8 (2008) (accepting answer that completed the record); California Indep. Operator Corp., 105
       FERC ¶ 61,284 at P 10 (2003) (accepting MISO’s answer that clarified the issues).
5
       Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of American Transmission Company LLC (“ATC Answer”) at 8-9.
       (emphasis added).



                                                           3
         While MISO appreciates ATC’s willingness to revise its definition of Large Load to

coincide with MISO’s 50 MW Large Load threshold, ATC’s plan to implement its own study

processes, agreements, and operational requirements for Large Loads without also requiring, at a

minimum, compliance with MISO’s IRR requirements, ultimately could create a less stringent

standard for load within ATC’s footprint, resulting in operational risk. ATC’s proposal to use

MISO’s IRR criteria only “if ATC does not have applicable criteria on a given topic”6 would result

in ATC’s criteria preempting – not supplementing - MISO’s IRR criteria. Thus, even if there is

initial alignment because Transmission Customers connecting through ATC Transmission

Facilities must follow MISO’s filed Tariff, ATC’s framework could be used to justify actions by

large loads that deviate from MISO’s requirements, creating implementation challenges and

reliability concerns, as described in MISO’s Protest.7 Further, ATC’s framework establishes a

broad, “topic” based approach that could result in ambiguity and uncertainty as to whether a

proposed ATC rule encompasses a requirement also included in MISO’s Tariff requirements

without specific identification. This could result in MISO’s specific Tariff requirements being

preempted rather than being supplemented in instances where ATC determines that applicable

MISO criteria can be considered as part of the same “topic” proposed by ATC. Ultimately, this

will drive process uncertainty for large loads, Transmission Customers, and other stakeholders,

because it would be unclear which MISO requirements have been preempted and where that

preemption ends. This uncertainty is compounded by the fact that ATC does not propose to include

many of its requirements in filed tariff sheets or pro forma agreements.




6
    ATC Answer at p. 8.
7
    MISO Protest at 6-11.



                                                4
         In addition, ATC did not address MISO’s need for direct operational visibility into ATC

large loads. As MISO explained in its Comments and Protest, MISO needs the ability to require

information directly from the Large Load in real time in order to anticipate demand swings, commit

generation reliably, maintain reserve sufficiency, and manage real time system balance. 8 ATC’s

transmission facilities are part of the larger MISO Transmission System and large loads connection

through ATC Facilities will have impacts beyond their own facilities. Allowing large loads

connected to the ATC system to deviate from the generally-applicable MISO visibility and

monitoring requirements would impair MISO’s operation of the Transmission System.

        Finally, while ATC indicates its willingness to use MISO’s definition of “Computational

Load,” MISO’s associated rules would not universally apply under ATC’s framework. Instead,

ATC will “distinguish between computational loads and other large loads for power factor and

other requirements as deemed necessary by ATC.”9 This could create different requirements for

ATC-located large loads as the “as deemed necessary” language appears to invite ad hoc

determinations. A common definition of “Computational Load” is a critical prerequisite to a

uniform ruleset. Treating a large load on ATC’s system differently from a technically similar large

load elsewhere in the MISO footprint would risk shifting costs, as loads with more strict

requirements may bear costs of reliability impacts caused by loads with less strict requirements.

        B.      ATC’S Proposals Exceed the Limits of Local Planning Criteria and Would
                Result in Inconsistent Terms of Transmission Service.

        MISO acknowledges that large loads present new challenges and that, addressing the

concerns noted by the Commission in the Show Cause Order will require MISO to impose

requirements where it previously did not. Large load study, operational, and Transmission Service


8
    Comments and Protest of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO Protest”) at 8-10.
9
    ATC Answer at p. 8.



                                                      5
 Requirements will overlap with established local planning criteria, and MISO seeks to work with

its Transmission Owners to accommodate local planning criteria as part of its regional framework.

       However, several aspects of ATC’s proposed large load framework exceed the traditional

bounds of local planning criteria in that they supersede MISO’s Tariff requirements with

reliability, operational, and market consequences that accrue to the MISO region broadly, and not

exclusively to ATC. They also create uncertainty about the applicability of the requirements MISO

will shortly file related to any large load pro forma cost recovery agreements and/or transparency

related to the costs associated with large loads. More specifically, ATC’s framework addresses

cost allocation for ATC large loads beginning at 100 MW whereas MISO’s Large Load cost

allocation provisions will be applied to MISO defined Large Loads of 50 MW. This raises

important questions that would need to be addressed including: (1) how will ATC’s proposal

prevent cost shifts associated with loads between 50 MW – 100 MW and will this gap result in

disparate treatment of wholesale loads within the ATC footprint; (2) will ATC’s proposed

agreements address situations in which network upgrades for a specific ATC large load are needed

on another MISO Transmission Owner’s facilities outside of the ATC footprint; and (3) will

ATC’s agreements include necessary security provisions as contemplated by the Show Cause

Order? MISO’s upcoming filings establishing a pro forma agreement and large load cost

transparency will address these questions and would set minimum requirements that ATC’s large

load framework could expand upon.

       The rules at issue here involve the processes for studying, pricing, granting, providing

transparency for, and maintaining system-wide operational reliability for Transmission Service.

There is room to accommodate and integrate local planning criteria while still maintaining a

uniform set of minimum requirements in such processes. However, for this room to exist, local




                                                6
 planning criteria must be supplemental to the uniform process and cannot overrule MISO’s

baseline requirements. While certain requirements that make sense for the MISO region may be

more than what any singular entity believes is needed, a uniform regional process for granting and

providing transparency for the same products—such as Transmission Service—does not create

undue burdens, especially when specific baseline requirements can be augmented by local

planning criteria. Any burdens that exist must be weighed against the benefits of such regional

uniformity—specifically including fairness, transparency, consistency, the avoidance of cost

shifts, maintaining regional reliability, and promoting commercial certainty in the Midwest region.

        C.     A Transition Framework May Be Useful to Balance Speed of Ruleset
               Implementation with Uniformity.

        MISO recognizes ATC’s concern that it may take several months or longer for all of

MISO’s large load 205 filing to be accepted by the Commission, whereas ATC’s process is

available now. To the extent that ATC currently is processing large load additions using existing

processes or expects to receive new additions before MISO’s processes are accepted, it would be

reasonable to allow ATC to use those study processes and operational requirements that the

Commission does accept to process large load interconnections on an interim basis until such time

as MISO’s proposed processes are accepted by the Commission. This would be consistent with

the Commission’s priority of not disrupting existing commercial arrangements and would allow

ATC to move forward now without precluding the benefits of a consistent region-wide process.

As part of this transition, ATC could be allowed to utilize its rules for projects submitted prior to

when MISO’s requirements are effective and continue to use its local planning criteria to

supplement, not supplant, MISO requirements thereafter. Such an approach would avoid conflicts

between MISO’s Tariff and ATC’s local planning criteria and facilitate both speed and a smooth

transition.

V.        NOTICE AND SERVICE

          MISO has served a copy of this filing electronically, including attachments, upon each

person designated on the official service list compiled by the Secretary as well as on all Tariff

customers, MISO Members, Member representatives of transmission owners and non-

transmission owners, as well as all state commissions within the MISO Region and the

Organization of MISO States. The filing has been posted electronically on MISO’s website at

https://www.misoenergy.org/legal/ferc-filings/ for other interested parties in this matter.

VI.       CONCLUSION

          WHEREFORE, MISO respectfully requests that the Commission (i) accept this Answer;

and (ii) direct ATC to revise Attachment FF-ATCLLC as requested in MISO’s Limited Protest;

and (iii) to the extent that the Commission determines that a transition would alleviate process
